The Regulatory Co-operation Statement and partnership working agreements should set out circumstances where joint action may be sought.

What can an enforcement body do if their local partner isn’t working collaboratively with them?

Disagreements should be resolved locally through senior level engagement. To assist this, the partnership working agreements – and the Building Safety Regulator’s Regulatory Co-operation Statement – will be required to contain dispute resolution arrangements.

Where there are ongoing co-operation issues between bodies - which have not been resolved through local engagement - then the Secretary of State may consider issuing a direction, but this would be a last resort.

Will the partnership working agreements duplicate measures already outline in Local Remediation Acceleration Plans?

Some areas already have partnership working agreements, Local Remediation Acceleration Plans, protocols or memorandums of understanding in place.

Where joint working agreements are already in place, local authorities and fire and rescue authorities should assess existing arrangements, and make sure they meet the requirements set out in the bill and any accompanying guidance.

Construction product manufacturer redress: section 149

Overview

Section 149 of the Building Safety Act 2022 allows legal action to be brought against manufacturers of cladding products where those products have caused or contributed to a building being unfit for habitation and in need of remediation.

To establish liability, a claimant must show that a product was defective, failed to meet regulatory requirements, or was sold on the basis of misleading statements, and that its use caused the building to be unsafe. Claims are brought by those with a legal interest in the building, such as owners or leaseholders.

Section 149 has not worked as intended. Very few claims have been made and stakeholders report that the regime is complex, difficult to evidence, and too easily allows liability to be avoided in practice. Current problems with section 149 include:

it is difficult to prove liability in cases involving multiple products

manufacturers can rely on technical compliance arguments, even where products contributed to unsafe outcomes

there is no clear route for some parties in the construction sector, such as developers, to bring direct claims against manufacturers where they have funded remediation due to unsafe or mis‑sold products

As a result, many of those who acted to fix unsafe buildings have borne the costs themselves, while manufacturers are not contributing.

The bill will make it easier for those who have paid to fix unsafe buildings to recover those costs from the manufacturers responsible by simplifying the section 149 statutory conditions.

First, the bill will place a clearer focus on safety and conduct. Liability will now turn on whether a product was unsafe or whether there was misleading conduct, rather than narrow technical compliance arguments about defectiveness.

Second, the causation test will also be simplified. It will be enough to show that a product made more than a trivial contribution to a building being unsafe.

Third, developers and others who have funded remediation will be able to bring claims directly against manufacturers.

The bill will also confirm that courts can apply Building Liability Orders to section 149 claims, allowing liability to be extended to associated companies where it is just and equitable. Courts will also be able to require companies to provide relevant product information to support claims.

Together, these changes will ensure that those who have been affected by unsafe and mis-sold cladding products have a clear route to recover costs, and that responsibility for remediation is shared more fairly across those who contributed to the problem.

Section 149 will continue to operate through the civil courts. Where liability is established, courts may require manufacturers to pay damages, including the costs of remediation linked to their products.

Implementation of construction product manufacturer redress: section 149

The changes will come into force 2 months after Royal Assent. They will apply to new claims and to cases already underway at that point, within the existing 30-year limitation period under the Building Safety Act 2022. These reforms will apply UK-wide, bringing Northern Ireland into scope for the first time.

No secondary legislation or statutory guidance is planned.

Will making it easier to bring claims lead to manufacturers becoming insolvent?

The reforms do not create automatic liability or guarantee claims will be successful. All claims must still be tested and proven through the courts, and will arise only where a manufacturer’s products have contributed to building safety failures.

The intention is not to penalise responsible businesses, but to ensure that those who supplied unsafe or mis‑sold products are held accountable.

Will this slow down remediation?

The reforms are designed to support remediation. The changes will create a better route to recover costs after remediation has taken place. Parties cannot rely on potential claims to defer or avoid their responsibility to remediate.

Developers and others who have committed to fix buildings, including through the Developer Remediation Contract, remain expected to do so. That position is unchanged. This provision is about how costs are recovered.

Medium-rise (11 to 18 metre) building register

Overview

The Building Safety Act 2022 required the Building Safety Regulator to create a register of 18 metres plus residential buildings – defined in the act as ‘higher-risk buildings’. This means the government should now have a complete record of higher-risk buildings in England, making it easier to identify those with potentially unsafe cladding.

These arrangements will operate alongside existing enforcement mechanisms, rather than replace them. The measure will apply to both new and existing Remediation Orders, made before the provisions come into effect, but only where there is continuing non-compliance.

The bill will also clarify that no limitation period under the Limitation Act 1980 applies to Remediation Orders, Remediation Contribution Orders and Building Liability Orders. Corresponding provision is made in relation to Wales.

This will provide certainty as to the availability of these remedies and help ensure that unsafe buildings can be remediated and that leaseholders and other interested persons can continue to access these protections.

The provisions for England will come into force 2 months following Royal Assent of the bill, and the detailed operation of the regime, will be set out in secondary legislation. Separate provision is made in relation to Wales.

Why is the penalty set at a maximum of £500,000?

The £500,000 cap is designed to strike a balance between providing a strong deterrent and ensuring proportionality in individual cases, with the tribunal retaining discretion to set the penalty. This allows the tribunal to flexibility impose higher penalties, within the £500,000 cap, in more serious cases.

Importantly, this is not a one-off penalty as landlords are still expected to comply with the original Remediation Order. Where a landlord continues to fail to comply with a Remediation Order, successive penalties can be imposed by the tribunal.

Protecting Remediation Contribution Order funds in trust

Remediation Contribution Orders were introduced under the Building Safety Act 2022 to make sure residents, local authorities and regulators can obtain funding to fix building safety defects through a court order requiring liable parties (developers and/or persons associated with them) to pay. However, there are no controls on how these funds are held. If a recipient (for example, a landlord) subsequently entered insolvency proceedings, Remediation Contribution Order remediation funds could be distributed to creditors as a priority under insolvency law. This creates a risk that funds may not be used for the purposes specified in the Order and that remediation is not accomplished. Because a Remediation Contribution Order represents the settlement of a claim, leaseholders will not be able to bring a further claim against the same party in future.

This measure will require Remediation Contribution Order to be held in a trust. The trust will protect remediation funds for remediation of building safety defects and ensure they are used for the purposes intended, even if a recipient, such as the landlord, obtains the funds and then subsequently becomes insolvent.

This new requirement will come into force shortly after royal assent by way of commencement regulations, to allow time for relevant changes to be made to the civil procedure rules and practice directions for the courts. We will also publish guidance for trustees on how to establish and manage the trust funds.

Who can be a trustee and what is their role?

The Remediation Contribution Order applicant may decide that the company or individual responsible for repairing the building (freeholder, management company, or head lessee) is best placed to act as the trustee of funds.

The trustee will be responsible for holding the sums in a trust fund for the purpose of making the payments referred to in the order.

How much will the trusts cost applicants?

We will provide that the First-tier Tribunal can award costs for establishing the trust account as part of the Remediation Contribution Order. If for any reason funds are not sufficient, it would be open to the applicants to return to the tribunal to request that they vary the order.

Notification of regulators

The insolvency of a Responsible Person can have implications for the safe management of a building which is subject to the Building Safety Act or Fire Safety Order regimes. Section 125A of the Building Safety Act 2022 (as amended by section 119 of the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024) puts a duty on Insolvency Practitioners who are appointed to the insolvency of a Responsible Person for a residential building, which is at least 5 storeys or 11 metres plus high, to notify local regulators (local authorities and fire and rescue services). In the case of higher-risk buildings (buildings which are at least 7 storeys or 18 metres plus in height), the Building Safety Regulator must also be notified. This ensures regulators are aware of the situation and can, at their discretion engage with both the Insolvency Practitioner and/or residents to check that the building is being safely managed during insolvency proceedings.

The Bill will extend this notification requirement to 2 further possible types of insolvency:

voluntary arrangements (an agreement to pay off some or all of their debts through an insolvency professional)

moratorium (a temporary timeframe giving an entity immunity from creditors to plan their financial affairs)

The Bill will require Responsible Persons for buildings of 11 metres or more in height who enter into voluntary arrangements or moratoriums to notify relevant regulators within 14 calendar days. They will need to provide high-level details about themselves, their financial situation, and the relevant building or buildings for which they are the Responsible Person.

Where enforcement action is required, there are important safeguards to ensure it remains fair and proportionate. Regulators must take account of the circumstances of each case, including whether there is a reasonable excuse for any failure to comply, such as delays arising from factors outside a responsible entity’s control. In addition, before imposing a financial penalty on a leaseholder-controlled company, regulators will be required to have regard to statutory guidance, including on whether alternative enforcement tools may be more appropriate. Together, these measures help ensure that enforcement is targeted at those failing to meet their responsibilities, while protecting those acting responsibly to make their buildings safe.

The Remediation Backstop

Overview

Relevant duty-holders have always been responsible for making their buildings safe from fire safety risks. Where they do not, fines and penalties can be a suitable sanction.

However, these sanctions do not guarantee the building will be fixed. The Remediation Backstop will operate as a final safety net where existing enforcement and available funding have not resulted in the building’s duty-holder (the person who is obliged to repair it) carrying out necessary remediation works. The existing duty-holder may have failed to comply with enforcement action taken against them, or with the legal duty to remediate. In these circumstances, local authorities or Homes England (remediation authorities) may be able to carry out the required remediation works instead.

To carry out these works, remediation authorities will be allowed to access funds from the government remediation schemes. Remediation authorities may also be able to apply for short-term assistance to meet additional administrative and legal costs associated with the backstop. These additional costs will then be recoverable from duty-holders once remediation has been completed.

Use of the Remediation Backstop

Examples of compliance failures which could trigger the backstop include:

a notice requiring removal or alteration of offending work under section 36 of the Building Act 1984

an Improvement Notice served by local authorities under the Housing Act 2004

an Enforcement Notice served by the local fire and rescue authority under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005

a Compliance Notice served under sections 99 to 100 of the Building Safety Act 2022 or section 36 of the Building Act 1984

a Remediation Order issued by the First-tier Tribunal (FTT) under the Building Safety Act 2022

a failure to comply with the legal duty to remediate

Where the duty-holder does not comply with a notice, an order, or the legal duty to remediate, the relevant regulator will be able to choose to take further punitive action, such as issuing fines or seeking a prosecution. Where the regulator believes there is no realistic path to remediation by the current duty-holder, it will be able to refer the case to the relevant local authority or to Homes England (as the designated ‘remediation authorities’) to consider a Remediation Management Order.

Where the remediation authority believes that a building might be suitable for the backstop, it will need to first serve a remediation notice on the duty-holder.

The notice will give the duty-holder 3 months to provide information about any steps it has already taken towards remediating life-critical external wall defects. The notice will also allow 3 months for the duty-holder (and other relevant persons who received the notice) to provide representations as to why they believe the backstop should not be considered for the building.

If the remediation authority decides to proceed with the backstop, it will need to apply to an FTT for a Remediation Management Order.

Remediation Management Orders

If the tribunal makes a Remediation Management Order, the remediation authority will be given powers to carry out the remedial works.

For its duration, a Remediation Management Order will allow the remediation authority to do anything that the duty-holder could ordinarily do for the purpose of assessing and remediating the external walls. For instance, the remediation authority will likely be granted access rights and the rights to deal with third parties (for example, by managing and entering into contracts) when necessary. The Order may also suspend the powers of the duty-holder.

While the Order is in force, the remediation authority may have some responsibility for managing the building on a day-to-day basis, depending on the terms. This means that, in addition to undertaking remediation work, the remediation authority may also be responsible for ensuring that some of the building services continue to operate whilst the Order is in place.

No fixed timescale for the Order will be prescribed by the tribunal. Once the works recommended by the FRAEW have been completed, a post-works assessment will be conducted. Provided this is satisfactory, the remediation authority will be expected to apply to the tribunal to discharge the Order, and the management of the building will revert to the control of the duty-holder.

Cost recovery

The remediation authority will cover the cost of remediation work through existing government remediation schemes. The duty-holder will be expected to repay additional costs incurred as a result of a Remediation Management Order where these were not covered by existing funds. All such repayable costs are expected to attract interest.
